title: Common ground: what both authors accept
subtitle: Cross-Text Connections

sections.heading: Where this sits for you
body: This pattern appears rarely. Learn to recognise it, but do not spend a session on it.

sections.heading: How to spot it
body: You are looking at this pattern when:
- The question says 'Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?' or asks what the two authors share.
- The texts usually disagree about the main claim, so you have to find the assumption underneath that both rely on.

sections.heading: The method
body: - 1) State the disagreement in one line, e.g. whether X causes Y or when Z began.
- 2) List what both texts take for granted: that the phenomenon exists, that it matters, or that it is hard to measure.
- 3) Pick the choice that each text supports with a sentence you can point to.
- If either text is silent on it, cut it.

sections.heading: What it is built to catch
body: You pick a statement that one author clearly holds and the other never addresses.
Worse, you pick one of the two sides of the disagreement itself.
Each choice has to pass a check against both texts separately.

sections.heading: You are losing these
body: Before you choose, say out loud what the question is asking for — not what you solved for.
You pick a statement that one author clearly holds and the other never addresses.
Worse, you pick one of the two sides of the disagreement itself.
